title: CELPIP General Listening — Practice Test 17
instructions: Listen to the audio for each part and answer the questions. Each audio plays once.

parts.title: Problem Solving
parts.description: A conversation in which one person has a problem and seeks help from another.

parts.title: Daily Life Conversation
parts.description: An everyday conversation between two people.

parts.title: Listening for Information
parts.description: An informational talk; listen for specific details.

parts.title: Discussion
parts.description: A discussion among people with different viewpoints.

parts.title: Viewpoints
parts.description: A longer talk presenting one speaker's opinion and reasons.

listeningScripts.title: A Cancelled Course and a Materials Fee
listeningScripts.text: Caller: I signed up for the woodworking course that was meant to start last Monday, and I've had an email saying it's cancelled. I've been refunded the tuition but not the materials fee. Office: Let me pull it up. Which course code? Caller: W-two-forty. The evening one. Office: Right, that one didn't run. Eleven registered, and we need fourteen. Caller: That's fair enough. But the materials fee is ninety dollars, and it's marked non-refundable. Office: Non-refundable applies when you withdraw. It doesn't apply when we cancel. If we cancel, everything goes back. Caller: The email didn't say that. Office: No, and it should. The template we use for cancellations is the same one we use for withdrawals, and that is a problem we have been told about before. Caller: So how do I get the ninety back? Office: I can request it now. It goes back to the card you paid with, and that takes about five business days. What I can't do is put it towards the winter session automatically, if that is what you would rather. That is a separate request and it has to come from you in writing. Caller: Is there any advantage to doing that? Office: There is, actually. A credit held against the winter session holds your place before registration opens, and W-two-forty in winter filled in two days last year. Caller: Then I would rather do that. Office: Then email registrations, say credit rather than refund, and quote the course code. Do it before Friday, because after Friday the refunds run automatically and I would have to reverse it.

listeningScripts.title: A House-Sit and the Cat
listeningScripts.text: A: You're away the first part of March, aren't you? B: Fourteenth to the twenty-eighth. Why? A: Because I'm away the second week of April, and I wondered whether we should do each other's houses rather than paying somebody. B: I'd take that. What does yours involve? A: Not much. Bins out on Tuesday, plants twice, and Mabel. B: Mabel is the cat that hates me. A: Mabel is the cat that hates everybody. She hides for three days and then she wants company constantly. You don't have to do anything except food twice a day and the litter tray. B: And medication? A: One tablet in the morning, in her food. She's had it for two years and she has never once noticed. B: Fine. Mine is easier — no animals. But the boiler needs the pressure topped up whenever it drops below one, and it does, about every ten days. A: Show me how before you go. Not over the phone from the airport. B: Agreed. And I would rather you stayed over than dropped in. The house being empty overnight is the thing I actually worry about. A: I'll stay over. Same at mine, if you can. Mabel gets destructive.

listeningScripts.title: Household Hazardous Waste Drop-Off
listeningScripts.text: Thanks for coming. This is the drop-off briefing, it takes six minutes, and it exists because over the last two years we have had things arrive here that could have hurt somebody. Opening hours are Thursday to Saturday, nine until four. We close for the last half hour to sort, so the last vehicle through the gate is half past three, not four. That is the single thing people get wrong. What we take: paint, solvents, motor oil, batteries of every kind, fluorescent tubes, garden chemicals, and medicines — although medicines are better taken to a pharmacy, because a pharmacy will take them any day of the week. What we do not take: explosives of any kind, including flares and old ammunition. Those go to the police, not to us. And no unlabelled containers. If you cannot tell us what is in it, we cannot tell the contractor what is in it, and the contractor will refuse the entire load. Keep everything in its original container if you possibly can. If you have decanted something, label it in permanent marker, and do not use a drinks bottle. A solvent in a lemonade bottle is the most dangerous thing that arrives here. Batteries: tape over the terminals of anything lithium. A loose lithium battery in a box of other batteries is how the depot in the next county burned down in the spring. And stay in your vehicle at the sorting bay. Our staff will unload for you. That is not us being precious. It is because you do not know what is already in the bay.

listeningScripts.title: Halifax Overnight Winter Parking Ban
listeningScripts.text: Halifax will bring in an overnight on-street parking ban from the first of December to the thirty-first of March, replacing the present system in which a ban is declared only when snow is forecast. Under the new rule, parking is prohibited on all streets from one until six in the morning for the whole four months, whether or not snow is expected. The city says the declared-ban system produced compliance of about sixty per cent, largely because residents did not reliably hear the declaration, and that plows were being sent down streets they could not clear. Fines rise from fifty dollars to a hundred, and towing will be used on designated snow routes only. Two councillors voted against, arguing that a four-month blanket ban penalises households without a driveway in the older parts of the city, where on-street parking is the only option. The city's own figures put the number of such households at about nine thousand. Staff said a permit scheme for those areas will be brought forward in the autumn, before the ban takes effect.

listeningScripts.title: Replacing the Boiler With a Heat Pump
listeningScripts.text: Vargas: The boiler is twenty-two years old and it has failed twice this winter. We have to do something before next October. Pelletier: Like for like is forty thousand. The heat pump quote is a hundred and ten. Diallo: With a grant of forty-five, so seventy-five net against forty. The gap is thirty-five thousand, and it pays back in running costs in about nine years. Pelletier: Nine years, on a building we have talked about selling twice. Vargas: We have talked about it and decided against it twice. Pelletier: Which is not the same as never selling it. Diallo: There is a real issue underneath all this, though, and it isn't the money. The heat pump only reaches its numbers if the hall holds heat, and that hall has single glazing on the north side and no loft insulation at all. Put a heat pump into that building today and it will run flat out and disappoint everybody. Vargas: So what's the sequence? Diallo: Insulation and glazing first. That's about eighteen thousand, and it pays for itself whichever heating you end up with. Then the heat pump next summer. Pelletier: And this winter? Diallo: Repair the boiler again. Three thousand or so, and it buys you one more season. It isn't wasted money if it buys the year you need to do the fabric properly. Vargas: I can defend three thousand this winter. I could not defend a hundred and ten thousand in October. Pelletier: Then that's the motion. Repair now, fabric in the spring, and the heat pump quoted again next summer with the fabric done.

listeningScripts.title: Ending Library Late Fines
listeningScripts.text: Hundreds of library systems have stopped charging late fines over the past decade, and the argument about it is a good example of a debate where the intuitive objection turns out to be the wrong one, and the real cost sits somewhere else entirely. The intuitive objection is that without a fine, nobody brings anything back. It is a reasonable thing to expect, and it is not what happens. Systems that dropped fines report return rates within a percentage point or two of what they were before. What keeps books coming back is not the fine. It is the hold on the account — you cannot borrow again until you return what you already have — and that stays in place. The fine was never the mechanism. The revenue objection is more serious than enthusiasts admit and smaller than it sounds. Fines were typically under two per cent of a library's budget, and a good part of that was consumed by the cost of collecting them: staff time at the desk, the payment system, the arguments. Several systems found that going fine-free was roughly cost-neutral once collection costs came out. So why do it at all? Because of who the fines fell on. The pattern is consistent everywhere it has been measured. Fines do not spread evenly. They concentrate on the branches in the poorest neighbourhoods, and the effect there is not a slow payment. It is a blocked card, and a household that stops coming. A library that has priced out the people who most need a free building has mislaid the point of itself. Where I would push back on the enthusiasts is the framing. This is not a policy that makes a library more efficient, and pretending that it is invites a budget officer to ask where the savings went. It costs a little, it is worth it, and it should be argued for on those terms.

questions.prompt: Why is the caller telephoning?
options: A course started without her being told
A materials fee was not returned when the course was cancelled
She has been refunded less tuition than she paid
She wants to withdraw from a course before it begins
questions.correctAnswer: A materials fee was not returned when the course was cancelled
questions.explanation: The tuition came back but the ninety-dollar materials fee did not, which is what the caller is querying.

questions.prompt: Why did the course not run?
options: The instructor was unavailable
The workshop was double-booked
Fourteen registered and eleven withdrew
Eleven people registered and fourteen were needed
questions.correctAnswer: Eleven people registered and fourteen were needed
questions.explanation: The office says the course did not run because eleven registered against a minimum of fourteen.

questions.prompt: When does the non-refundable rule apply?
options: When the student withdraws, not when the college cancels
To materials fees but never to tuition
Only after the course has begun
Whenever a course fills in under a week
questions.correctAnswer: When the student withdraws, not when the college cancels
questions.explanation: The office is clear that non-refundable covers a student withdrawing; when the college cancels, everything goes back.

questions.prompt: Why did the email give the wrong impression?
options: It was sent to the wrong student
It was written before the refund policy changed
The same template is used for cancellations and withdrawals
The materials fee was listed as tuition
questions.correctAnswer: The same template is used for cancellations and withdrawals
questions.explanation: The office admits the cancellation email uses the withdrawal template, and says this has been raised before.

questions.prompt: How long does a refund to the card take?
options: Until the winter session opens
About five business days
Until Friday of that week
About two days
questions.correctAnswer: About five business days
questions.explanation: A refund goes back to the card used and takes about five business days.

questions.prompt: What is the advantage of taking a credit instead?
options: It holds a place before registration opens
It is worth more than the fee that was paid
It can be used on any course in the college
It arrives faster than a refund
questions.correctAnswer: It holds a place before registration opens
questions.explanation: A credit held against the winter session holds the caller's place before registration opens — worth having, since the course filled in two days last winter.

questions.prompt: What must the caller's email say?
options: The date of the cancelled class
The amount of the materials fee
That she accepts the non-refundable terms
Credit rather than refund, with the course code
questions.correctAnswer: Credit rather than refund, with the course code
questions.explanation: The office asks for an email to registrations saying credit rather than refund, and quoting the course code.

questions.prompt: Why must it be sent before Friday?
options: The winter registration opens on Friday
The office closes for the week on Friday
After Friday the refunds are processed automatically
The credit expires at the end of the week
questions.correctAnswer: After Friday the refunds are processed automatically
questions.explanation: After Friday the refunds run automatically and the office would have to reverse one to create the credit.

questions.prompt: Why does A raise the subject?
options: A wants somebody to look after the cat permanently
A has been asked to house-sit by a neighbour
A is going away at the same time as B
A is away in April and would rather not pay somebody
questions.correctAnswer: A is away in April and would rather not pay somebody
questions.explanation: A is away the second week of April, against B's fourteenth to twenty-eighth of March, and suggests they cover each other's houses instead of paying.

questions.prompt: What does A's house need?
options: The bins out daily and the cat fed twice
The bins out, the plants watered twice, and the cat fed
The plants watered twice a day
Nothing beyond feeding the cat
questions.correctAnswer: The bins out, the plants watered twice, and the cat fed
questions.explanation: A lists bins on Tuesday, plants twice, and Mabel — who needs food twice a day, the litter tray and a tablet.

questions.prompt: What is said about the cat's medication?
options: It has to be given twice a day
It is difficult to get her to take it
A tablet goes in her food each morning and she has never noticed
It is only needed if she stops eating
questions.correctAnswer: A tablet goes in her food each morning and she has never noticed
questions.explanation: One tablet in the morning, in her food; she has taken it for two years without once noticing.

questions.prompt: What does B's house need?
options: The boiler pressure topped up when it falls
The plants watered every ten days
The heating turned off while B is away
Nothing at all, since there are no animals
questions.correctAnswer: The boiler pressure topped up when it falls
questions.explanation: B has no animals, but the boiler pressure drops below one about every ten days and needs topping up — which A asks to be shown before B leaves.

questions.prompt: What does B care about most?
options: That the boiler is checked every day
That the house is left tidy
That somebody sleeps in the house rather than calling in
That A arrives before the fourteenth
questions.correctAnswer: That somebody sleeps in the house rather than calling in
questions.explanation: B would rather A stayed over than dropped in, because the house standing empty overnight is what actually worries B.

questions.prompt: When is the last vehicle allowed through the gate?
options: Four o'clock
Nine o'clock
Half past three
Half an hour before closing on Saturdays only
questions.correctAnswer: Half past three
questions.explanation: The site is open nine until four but closes for the last half hour to sort, so the gate shuts to vehicles at half past three — the thing the speaker says people most often get wrong.

questions.prompt: Why does the gate close before the site does?
options: The last half hour is used for sorting
Staff need time to unload the final vehicles
The contractor collects at that time
The bay has to be cleared for the next day
questions.correctAnswer: The last half hour is used for sorting
questions.explanation: The half hour between the gate closing and the site closing is for sorting what has been dropped off.

questions.prompt: Where does the speaker say medicines are better taken?
options: To the depot, but only on a Thursday
To the police, with any other controlled items
Anywhere, provided they are in the original packet
To a pharmacy, which accepts them on any day
questions.correctAnswer: To a pharmacy, which accepts them on any day
questions.explanation: The depot will take medicines, but the speaker recommends a pharmacy instead because a pharmacy accepts them any day of the week.

questions.prompt: What happens if a container is unlabelled?
options: It is opened and identified by staff
The contractor refuses the whole load
It is held until the owner identifies it
It is treated as an explosive
questions.correctAnswer: The contractor refuses the whole load
questions.explanation: If the depot cannot tell the contractor what is in a container, the contractor refuses the entire load — which is why unlabelled containers are not accepted at all.

questions.prompt: What must be done with lithium batteries?
options: They must be brought in their original packaging
They must be handed to staff separately
The terminals must be taped over
They are not accepted at the depot
questions.correctAnswer: The terminals must be taped over
questions.explanation: Lithium batteries need their terminals taped; a loose one among other batteries is how the depot in the next county burned down in the spring.

questions.prompt: Why must people stay in their vehicles at the sorting bay?
options: They cannot know what is already in the bay
Staff are insured only for their own handling
The bay is too narrow for two people
Vehicles must be moved quickly at busy times
questions.correctAnswer: They cannot know what is already in the bay
questions.explanation: The speaker gives the reason directly: it is not about ceremony, but that a member of the public does not know what is already sitting in the bay.

questions.prompt: What is changing?
options: A ban declared when snow is forecast replaces a nightly one
A ban every night replaces one declared when snow is forecast
Overnight parking becomes free on all streets
The winter parking season is extended by four months
questions.correctAnswer: A ban every night replaces one declared when snow is forecast
questions.explanation: The new rule prohibits on-street parking from one until six every night from December to March, in place of the declared-ban system.

questions.prompt: What was the problem with the old system?
options: It applied for too much of the year
Fines were too high to be enforced
Snow routes were left uncleared entirely
Only about sixty per cent of drivers complied
questions.correctAnswer: Only about sixty per cent of drivers complied
questions.explanation: The city says the declared-ban system produced compliance of about sixty per cent, so plows were being sent down streets they could not clear.

questions.prompt: What does the city give as the reason for that?
options: The fines were rarely issued
Declarations were made too late in the day
Residents did not reliably hear the declaration
Residents had nowhere else to park
questions.correctAnswer: Residents did not reliably hear the declaration
questions.explanation: The low compliance is put down largely to residents not reliably hearing that a ban had been declared.

questions.prompt: What was the two councillors' objection?
options: It penalises households that have no driveway
The fine of a hundred dollars is too low
Towing should apply on every street
Four months is not long enough
questions.correctAnswer: It penalises households that have no driveway
questions.explanation: The two who voted against argued that a four-month blanket ban falls on households without a driveway in older parts of the city, where the street is the only option — about nine thousand households.

questions.prompt: What did staff undertake to do?
options: Review the fine after the first winter
Publish the compliance figures each month
Exempt the older parts of the city
Bring forward a permit scheme before the ban starts
questions.correctAnswer: Bring forward a permit scheme before the ban starts
questions.explanation: Staff said a permit scheme for those areas will be brought forward in the autumn, before the ban takes effect.

questions.prompt: Why does something have to be done?
options: The boiler is twenty-two years old and has failed twice this winter
The grant expires in October
The hall has been condemned as too cold
The centre has been told to cut its emissions
questions.correctAnswer: The boiler is twenty-two years old and has failed twice this winter
questions.explanation: Vargas opens with a twenty-two-year-old boiler that has failed twice this winter, and a deadline of next October.

questions.prompt: What is the difference in cost once the grant is counted?
options: Seventy thousand
A hundred and ten thousand
Thirty-five thousand
Forty-five thousand
questions.correctAnswer: Thirty-five thousand
questions.explanation: A hundred and ten thousand less a forty-five thousand grant is seventy-five net, against forty thousand for a like-for-like boiler: a gap of thirty-five thousand.

questions.prompt: What is Pelletier's objection to the nine-year payback?
options: Nine years is longer than the heat pump will last
The building might be sold before nine years are up
The running-cost figures are unreliable
The grant may not be renewed
questions.correctAnswer: The building might be sold before nine years are up
questions.explanation: Pelletier's point is that nine years is a long payback on a building the committee has twice discussed selling — and that deciding against it twice is not the same as never selling.

questions.prompt: What does Diallo say the real issue is?
options: The grant conditions are too restrictive
The committee cannot agree on a timetable
Heat pumps are unsuited to public buildings
The hall does not hold heat well enough
questions.correctAnswer: The hall does not hold heat well enough
questions.explanation: Diallo sets the money aside: a heat pump only reaches its numbers if the building holds heat, and this one does not.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with the building?
options: Single glazing on one side and no loft insulation
A roof that leaks above the hall
Radiators too small for a heat pump
No space for the outdoor unit
questions.correctAnswer: Single glazing on one side and no loft insulation
questions.explanation: The hall has single glazing on the north side and no loft insulation at all, so a heat pump installed today would run flat out and disappoint everybody.

questions.prompt: Why does Diallo want the insulation done first?
options: It is a condition of the grant
It costs less than repairing the boiler
The heat pump cannot be installed until it is done
It pays for itself whatever heating is chosen
questions.correctAnswer: It pays for itself whatever heating is chosen
questions.explanation: The fabric work is about eighteen thousand and pays for itself whichever heating system the centre ends up with, which is what makes it the first step rather than a delay.

questions.prompt: What is proposed for this winter?
options: Installing the heat pump before October
Repairing the boiler again for about three thousand
Closing the hall for the coldest months
Doing the insulation immediately
questions.correctAnswer: Repairing the boiler again for about three thousand
questions.explanation: Diallo's proposal for the winter is another boiler repair at about three thousand, buying one more season.

questions.prompt: Why does Diallo say that money is not wasted?
options: The repair is covered by the grant
The parts can be reused in the heat pump
It buys the year needed to do the fabric properly
The boiler will be sold with the building
questions.correctAnswer: It buys the year needed to do the fabric properly
questions.explanation: The repair is not wasted because it buys the year in which the insulation and glazing can be done, which the heat pump depends on.

questions.prompt: What is the objection the speaker calls intuitive?
options: That libraries will lose most of their income
That borrowers will take out more than they need
That staff will have nothing to enforce
That books will not be returned
questions.correctAnswer: That books will not be returned
questions.explanation: The intuitive objection is that without a fine nobody brings anything back — reasonable to expect, and not what the evidence shows.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say actually brings books back?
options: Reminder messages sent before the due date
Being unable to borrow again until the item is returned
The fine, in systems that still charge one
The threat of losing membership altogether
questions.correctAnswer: Being unable to borrow again until the item is returned
questions.explanation: Return rates barely move, because the mechanism was never the fine: it is the hold on the account, which stays in place after fines end.

questions.prompt: What share of a library's budget did fines typically represent?
options: Under two per cent
Under ten per cent
About a fifth
It varied too much to say
questions.correctAnswer: Under two per cent
questions.explanation: Fines were typically under two per cent of the budget, and a good part of that went on collecting them.

questions.prompt: Why was going fine-free roughly cost-neutral for several systems?
options: Borrowing rose enough to attract more funding
Fewer books were lost once fines ended
Collecting the fines used up much of what they raised
The saving was replaced by a donation scheme
questions.correctAnswer: Collecting the fines used up much of what they raised
questions.explanation: Staff time at the desk, the payment system and the arguments consumed a good part of the fine income, so several systems found the change roughly cost-neutral.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker give as the real reason to end fines?
options: They take more staff time than any other task
They are collected inconsistently from one branch to another
They are unpopular with library staff
They fall hardest on the poorest neighbourhoods and block cards there
questions.correctAnswer: They fall hardest on the poorest neighbourhoods and block cards there
questions.explanation: The pattern is consistent wherever measured: fines concentrate on branches in the poorest neighbourhoods, and the result is a blocked card and a household that stops coming.

questions.prompt: Where does the speaker disagree with supporters of the policy?
options: In claiming that return rates are unaffected
In presenting it as a saving rather than a cost worth paying
In wanting it introduced everywhere at once
In expecting other library systems to follow quickly
questions.correctAnswer: In presenting it as a saving rather than a cost worth paying
questions.explanation: The speaker's caution is about framing: it is not an efficiency measure, and calling it one invites a budget officer to ask where the savings went. It costs a little and is worth it.
